source.title: Why is SAM Robust to Label Noise?
source.authors: Christina Baek; Zico Kolter; Aditi Raghunathan

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures training accuracy during training on CIFAR-10 with random label corruption, using SAM variants and SGD. It does not directly test the broader claim about reaching near-zero training error across sufficiently large networks and benchmarks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-accuracy curves in Figure 1 and states that SAM achieves higher clean training accuracy before fitting noisy data. Other results about test accuracy and regularization do not directly measure the training-error claim.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 measures training classification accuracy for a randomly initialized convolutional network trained with SGD on corrupted-label CIFAR-10, directly bearing on V1. The supplied figure text does not establish the final training-error level.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Explicit logit reweighting explains the linear-model result, whereas Jacobian perturbation preserves nearly all of SAM's robustness in the tested neural networks. Analysis and interventions implicate regularization of intermediate activations and final-layer weights, affecting early learning rather than merely flatness at convergence.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares 1-SAM and SGD on noisy CIFAR-10 and analyzes early-stopping accuracy and training dynamics; it does not reproduce the original claim’s training-error evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The study focuses on 1-SAM; its Figure 1 result distinguishes clean from noisy training examples and compares SAM with SGD. CIFAR-10 experiments replace Batch Norm with Layer Norm.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports best test accuracy of 69.47% for 1-SAM, 52.48% for SGD, and 60.8% for regularized SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM and partial approximations to its regularization improve early-stopping generalization under label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.3 reports unstable 1-SAM optimization with batch normalization and replaces it with layer normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-example SAM perturbations can be incompatible with the batch-normalized training setup used here; this does not measure V6's training-speed or learning-rate advantage.

record.problems: The relevant Figure 1 training-accuracy values are presented graphically without exact values in the text. The reported setup is limited to CIFAR-10 with 30% label corruption and ResNet18.
record.rows_left_out: No other results directly measure the claim’s training-error outcome. Test-accuracy comparisons and regularization results measure generalization performance, not training classification error.

untested.parts: Near-zero final training error is unresolved in the supplied figure text. CIFAR-100, fully randomized labels, Adam, and systematic capacity or regularization comparisons using training error are not tested. The study does use randomly corrupted labels.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts.
Initialization comparisons measuring training speed or trainable depth.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to the initial or evolving stability threshold.
Matched comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance with and without batch normalization, or with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope label: failure to establish near-zero error is an evidential gap, not an observed failure of V1. Figure 1's relative learning trajectories do not supply a readable final training-error verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test CIFAR-100, random labels, Adam, or whether sufficiently large models reach zero or near-zero training error after long training.
